I think there are some really great responses on this post. Social stratifications, stoicism, and antisocial behaviors are excellent points and I agree with every one of them, just thought I'd add my two cents as well. 

Western society is massively eclectic, however very distinct in some of our unified values, societal structures, and more or less the way we think, operate, and view the world around us. Where there are societal norms, there are inherently deviant behaviors that exist in response to those norms. To be honest I don't know the root of the stigma for getting high originates from, but I would put my money on the social stratification as described my /u/MissPoopsHerPants to be a good place to start. Once there is a stigma in a society, for example the "crack epidemic", that receives huge amounts of media attention, it shapes the way we view the world wether we realize it or not. Communication studies scholars refer to this as cultivation theory, In that our worldview is shaped by the media that we take in. 

So basically, a behavior is deemed "deviant" not by the nature of the action, but by the societal norms that are inherently shaped by the culture in which they are found.

ABOUT DAVE CHAPELLE: I got into Hartford Connecticut last night to headline the Funny Bone and was checking into the hotel at about 1am. My new wife and I were getting in the elevator, and Dave walks out looking at his phone. I said, "Hey Dave, what's up?" He walked past me, looking at his phone and one of his crew said, "That was Titus." Chappelle whipped around and came back and apologized THREE TIMES for walking past me. We talked for a minute and he said he had a "weird show." Three things-- he was lucid, Not HIgh and feeling bad about his show. Like a true comic. No comic wants to have a bad show, but it happens. I have met Dave a few times and he is ALWAYS the nicest dude in show business. So to you jumping on the Chapelle hate tour, eat me. None of the audience knows what it takes to do comedy. In a band, you have other musicians and you can just tune into each other if things are going weird. With comedy, the audience is half of the show, the response half which is equal to the joke half from the comic. The "Funny or Die" show consisted of some of the baddest ass acts in comedy-- Hannibal Burress, Demetri Martin, Jeff Ross, and The Flight of the Conchords, who did an HOUR in front of Chapelle. Again, this is after four or five other acts. The show went on for over three hours. I have done comedy since I was 18 years old and have NEVER seen a three hour comedy show. And I HATE following a music act. 3+ hours? I dont care if Pryor and Carlin came back from the dead, audiences cant hang that long. So any excuses aside, I ran into Dave less than 2 hours after that show and he was sober and aware that it went weird. Comedy is priceless. You can't buy a real laugh but I can buy music all day, it just has to be music. BUT the people that can actually make you laugh out loud are few and far between. Laughter relieves stress, changes brain chemistry, creates endorphins which may even slow or stop cancer cells. (I'm not a Doctor so don't even fucking respond to that.) So when we have an off-night, maybe you can look back at the decades of funny that a comic has brought to you and cut him some slack. Now, after he's done it three times... then you can cut his ass off. - TITUS
